item.title: Monet Painting Sells for $56 Million in France
item.description:
A large Claude Monet painting of flowers in his Giverny water garden sold for 50 million euros (about $56 million) at Sotheby’s in Paris on Thursday.

After a 42-minute bidding tussle between at least six would-be buyers on telephones, the painting, titled “Iris,” was bought by an Asian client bidding by phone with Jen Hua, deputy chairman of Sotheby’s Asia.

“I’ve never seen bidding that long,” said Helly Nahmad, a London dealer who specializes in modern art.

“It was insane,” he added, “but these things are mega-rare.”

The world record for a Monet painting is $110.7 million, set in 2019 at Sotheby’s with the sale of the 1890 painting “Meules,” or “Grainstacks.” (The price would be $145.7 million today, adjusted for inflation.)

“Iris,” which is about 5 feet tall and nearly 6 feet wide, depicts flowers swaying above skies reflected in Monet’s famous lily pond. Experts think the canvas was painted in the open air in 1924-25, toward the end of the artist’s life. It had been estimated to sell for between €20 million to €30 million.

Until recently, owners of high-value artworks routinely consigned their trophies to auctions in either New York or London. But since Brexit has made Britain a less attractive destination for art sales, European collectors have been more willing to sell in Paris.

In March, Alon Zakaim, a London dealer, offered a rare pair of Monet “series” landscape paintings from the 1890s at TEFAF Maastricht, in the Netherlands, with an asking price of $20 million. They found a buyer after the fair.

“It was a pretty painting with a modern look that attracts new buyers,” Zakaim said of the painting sold on Thursday. “It relates well to later 20th-century works,” he added. “The appetite for these large, late Monet paintings is increasing.”

“Iris” had been in the collection of Jeanne Schlumberger, an heiress to the Schlumberger energy company, now known as SLB. During the 1950s and ’60s, with the help of the pioneering Paris dealer Katia Granoff, Schlumberger amassed an extensive collection of Impressionist and modern art, including late paintings by Monet, which were then out of fashion, according to Sotheby’s.

“Iris” was among about 50 Monets that Granoff bought from the artist’s son Michel in 1956. Schlumberger acquired it the following year.

“Once the painting arrived in her house, it left the world,” Thomas Bompard, a senior international specialist at Sotheby’s Paris, said in an interview before the auction. He said the painting had “never been exhibited.”

Schlumberger died in 1983, and her descendants have chosen the 100th anniversary of Monet’s death to sell “Iris” and 26 other works from her collection at Sotheby’s.

Cyrille de Gunzburg, a private dealer in Paris, said in an interview at the Sotheby’s pre-auction view that he had negotiated the sale of a Monet from a similar date for $15 million in 2013.

“Art history tells us that Cézanne was the big influence on Modern art,” he said. “Paintings like this show it was also Monet.”

In recent years, as Monet’s influence on Abstract Expressionism and other 20th-century art movements has been more widely appreciated, wealthy collectors have coveted the artist’s late works.

“This painting could be benchmarked against the great Monets in the museums of Paris,” said Helena Newman, Sotheby’s worldwide chairman of Impressionist & Modern art. “It was a true museum quality work.”

Overall, the Schlumberger collection raised €74.4 million, or about $83.5 million.

item.title: Fearing Mass A.I. Layoffs, Some in Congress Eye Ways to Aid Workers
item.description:
The rapid rise of artificial intelligence has stoked fears that powerful computers might someday replace humans, leaving millions of Americans out of work and without a steady income.

It’s a doomsday scenario, one that could potentially overwhelm the government’s ability to care for the swelling ranks of the unemployed. And the mere risk has caught the attention of Congress, where lawmakers are starting to explore ways to bolster the nation’s economic safety net before it is too late.

In recent months, Democrats and Republicans have unfurled a series of bills that aim to offset the potential job losses posed by the advent of A.I. The ideas may differ in scope and cost, but together they reflect a widening trepidation in Washington that the government has fallen behind in preparing for vast technological change.

The latest proposal is set to arrive this week: a bill from Democrats including Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who leads his party on the chamber’s chief tax-writing committee, that would greatly expand the nation’s unemployment insurance program.

Existing jobless benefits cover a fraction of out-of-work Americans’ wages, generally for up to 26 weeks. Under Mr. Wyden’s bill, Congress would provide additional aid in times of high unemployment. Plus, there would be up to 26 weeks of further assistance to help those displaced by technology to learn new skills.

The bill includes other upgrades to a key federal safety-net program whose strains were obvious — and largely unresolved — amid the pandemic. With A.I., Mr. Wyden said, there is growing urgency to address those deficiencies, as the nation readies for “one of the biggest economic impacts on the economy in American history.”

“I think it would be malpractice to not get ready, because we’re in a position now where many citizens feel the looming fear of A.I. job losses,” he said. “And Congress has a responsibility to help the country get ready.”

The arrival of A.I. represents a seminal political test for the nation’s capital, where policymakers racked by division are slow to act except in times of crisis. The dynamic offers a contrast with the breakneck pace of development in Silicon Valley, where many believe that A.I. could auger swift and tectonic economic disruptions.

Speaking at a global conference this month, a co-founder of Anthropic projected that U.S. output could rise by almost 50 percent by 2030. But that same company’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, has coupled rosy growth forecasts with more dire warnings that A.I. could upend millions of workers’ lives.

For now, economists see no evidence that A.I. has altered the labor market on a grand scale. But there are still some emerging “A.I.-related hiring headwinds,” according to a report this week from Goldman Sachs, which found it has contributed to slower-than-expected job growth recently in some industries sensitive to technological change.

Martha Gimbel, the executive director of the Yale Budget Lab, emphasized that the signs do not yet suggest that A.I. is having a macroeconomic effect. But she also stressed that the work to measure those changes in real time was both “historically unusual” and difficult.

“In the middle of the Industrial Revolution, people weren’t trying to guess whether the weavers had been displaced yet,” she said.

The uncertainty has started to gain attention in Washington, where Democrats and Republicans have found common cause around the basic idea that the government should find better ways to measure the effects of A.I.

One of those bills, written by Senators Josh Hawley, Republican of Missouri, and Mark Warner, Democrat of Virginia, would require more robust reporting from companies about A.I.-related layoffs.

“I actually believe over a longer haul, five years plus, A.I. will probably create whole new categories of jobs,” Mr. Warner said. “But what does that do for the interim? And we don’t have good data yet.”

Despite bipartisan support, the bill and other, similar measures have stalled on Capitol Hill, where Republicans have largely followed President Trump in adopting a hands-off approach to artificial intelligence.

Bret Swanson, a technology expert at the conservative-leaning Heritage Foundation, said the reticence might stem from the fact that Republicans did not want to do anything to “disrupt these huge investments into A.I., which are sustaining what may otherwise be a rocky economy.”

That, Mr. Swanson continued, has affected even the debate over the implications for workers, which could “draw attention to the downsides” of A.I. in the eyes of a skeptical nation.

Mr. Trump’s top aides have dismissed any suggestion that A.I. could cause mass layoffs. In contrast, many Democrats still see wide-scale unemployment as a growing threat, and in response, party leaders have pursued measures meant to help Americans affected by technological change.

The roster of bills includes an attempt by Senator Mark Kelly, Democrat of Arizona, to tax tech giants’ profits for a new federal trust. That would help fund benefits and training for displaced workers. Another, by lawmakers including Representative Greg Casar, Democrat of Texas, would tax tech companies and channel the proceeds to job-creating infrastructure investments.

But those efforts to boost the federal safety net face an even tougher political climb, given long-simmering disputes between the parties about the role of government and the provision of federal benefits. The result is a sort of stasis on Capitol Hill, despite a “high level of anxiety” on both sides of the aisle over job losses, according to Gina Raimondo, the leader of Raise Us, a nonprofit focused on A.I. policy.

“My great worry, actually, is that they’ll do what Congress often does, which is wait until it’s too late,” added Ms. Raimondo, whose group is backed by tech companies. She formerly served as commerce secretary under President Joseph R. Biden Jr.

There is also the thornier political question of who, exactly, should pay for it.

A handful of tech giants, including Anthropic and OpenAI, have publicly supported ideas that would set aside some of their expected new riches for Americans, especially those displaced by artificial intelligence. This week, Anthropic announced it would set aside a portion of its stock for a “public benefit fund,” and Elon Musk, the founder of SpaceX, followed by promising to give away shares to “every kid in America.”

Otherwise, most tech companies have steered clear of endorsing specific bills in Congress targeting tech wealth. In the meantime, these companies and their executives have committed millions of dollars toward trying to elect tech-friendly lawmakers in the midterm elections, despite growing voter resentment.

Mr. Wyden said he believed that backlash was “starting to open some eyes” in Silicon Valley. But he acknowledged that A.I. companies had not endorsed his new legislation, called the Stability and Opportunity for Workers Act. The measure is backed by other Democrats, including Michael Bennet of Colorado, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Chuck Schumer of New York.

If adopted, the bill would raise the minimum level of unemployment benefits, which vary by state but on average cover less than half of workers’ past wages, according to program advocates. It would also expand the pool of people eligible to receive aid.

For the moment, his proposal does not have an official cost estimate, and Mr. Wyden did not include a provision to pay for the benefits, which currently are funded by employer payroll taxes. In other legislation, he has called for taxing tech giants and their data centers as a way to ensure that “big companies play a role” in offsetting their burden.

Still, Mr. Wyden added of the new legislative push: “There’s a lot of work to do.”

item.title: How Trump Gave the Worst Polluters a Free Pass
item.description:
Middle schoolers on their way to class in the shadow of a flare from the Indorama Ventures chemical facility in Port Neches, Texas. Video by Meridith Kohut.

Supported by

The president temporarily waived clean-air rules for industrial facilities that spew cancer-causing gases. Then his appointees worked to gut the regulations altogether.

By Eric Lipton and Maxine Joselow

Graphics by Mira Rojanasakul

Eric Lipton reported from Port Neches, Texas. Maxine Joselow reported from Clairton, Pa., and Richmond, Va.

Within sight of a southeast Texas middle school stands a chemical plant that President Trump excused from new federal rules intended to curb its cancer-causing pollution.

About a 30-minute drive from Pittsburgh, a steel-making facility has spewed carcinogenic chemicals near homes for years. Mr. Trump gave it a similar waiver from recent clean-air rules.

And on the outskirts of Richmond, Va., the owners of an industrial warehouse emailed the Trump administration asking for their own waiver. Their wish was granted. Nine months later, the facility accidentally released a large plume of carcinogenic gas into the community.

In total, since taking office again, Mr. Trump exempted 202 facilities in 39 states and Puerto Rico from clean-air regulations that were going into effect. Some were among the country’s worst industrial polluters, including chemical manufacturers, copper smelters and coal-burning power plants. About 3.3 million people live within three miles of at least one affected facility.

0 coal plants, 0 chemical plants, 0 sterilizers, 0 steel-related facilities and 0 copper smelter exempted from clean-air regulations.

Note: The number of people near each facility was determined using the 2024 population in each census block-group within a three-mile radius of each plant. Block-groups that were partly within the radius were population-weighted with 2020 census block population counts. Source: Data from the Environmental Defense Fund and Environmental Integrity Project. The New York Times

The exemptions represent the biggest presidential intervention in enforcement of the Clean Air Act in the half-century since President Richard M. Nixon signed the bedrock environmental law. And that is only one of the ways the Trump administration is dismantling a variety of federal environmental protections.

Before Mr. Trump’s return, the chemical industry was losing its fight to block or at least delay tougher E.P.A. requirements to reduce toxic emissions. It had pleaded with agency officials, filed lawsuits and appealed to Congress. But officials and the courts had largely rejected the industry’s claims of undue expense and regulatory overreach.

Now, Mr. Trump is prioritizing the economic interests of corporations and easing costs for polluting industries, and their immense clout is striking.

The president’s exemptions were good for two years, with the possibility of an extension. The reprieve for the companies gave Mr. Trump time to stock the Environmental Protection Agency with appointees who had lobbied for the industries they now regulate. Those officials then quickly went to work from the inside to gut the rules altogether.

Mr. Trump has taken an expansive view of executive power in his second term. On the environmental front, he has unilaterally shredded regulations, withheld science funding appropriated by Congress and ordered coal plants that planned to shutter to continue running.

Even so, his evisceration of the new Clean Air Act rules stands out.

Many of the details of how the Trump administration aided the chemical industry are being reported here for the first time. In one upside-down moment, industry executives provided the agenda for a meeting with E.P.A. staff and then effectively presided over it.

Mr. Trump also nominated Aaron Szabo, a former lobbyist for the Advanced Medical Technology Association, or AdvaMed, a powerful trade group, to lead the E.P.A.’s air regulation office. Once there, Mr. Szabo helped handle the waiver requests and then pushed employees to pull back on enforcement, documents show.

To understand how Mr. Trump gave a free pass to some of the worst polluters, The New York Times reviewed more than 10,000 pages of government documents and spoke to more than 70 people familiar with the efforts, including former E.P.A. officials and industry executives.

“These companies, with their campaign contributions and the revolving door of former lobbyists and executives that now work in the regulatory agencies — that is where the petrochemical industry gets its power,” said Brent Coon, a Beaumont, Texas, lawyer who has spent decades squaring off in court against petrochemical firms over environmental and health risks.

The Clean Air Act requires the E.P.A. — created in 1970 to protect public health and the environment — to periodically review the latest pollution controls and impose them broadly if they are affordable and effective. The most recent review began under the Biden administration, which in 2024 finalized new, tougher requirements.

In granting the waivers to those rules, Mr. Trump cited an obscure clause in the act that allows exemptions if complying with new rules would threaten national security and if the necessary technology is not widely available.

Yet the president approved the waivers even though the equipment was readily accessible and the industry’s national security claims had little detail to substantiate them, documents show.

The Biden administration pushed through the new pollution requirements after evidence emerged about the health threats posed by ethylene oxide, a colorless gas used to make products like plastic soda bottles and to sterilize medical devices like pacemakers.

E.P.A. researchers had concluded that ethylene oxide was 30 to 60 times as carcinogenic as previously thought, particularly for people who live near plants where the gas is made or used. The agency held meetings to warn community members about the elevated risks.

Outside Richmond, home to one of the country’s largest commercial sterilizers of medical devices, some residents left one of these briefings wondering whether recent cancer diagnoses among neighbors were tied to the plant, though it is virtually impossible to prove pollution caused a specific cancer case.

“You see these pretty buildings, and you think they’re OK,” said Wayne Powell, who lives a five-minute drive from the plant, which resembles an ordinary warehouse. “But you don’t know that they’re harboring things that are hazardous to our health.”

As recently as April, the plant, owned by Sterilization Services of Virginia, had a mishap. A faulty valve caused 580 pounds of ethylene oxide to leak from large drums and waft in a toxic plume over nearby homes, state records show. The plant’s state permit allows it to discharge no more than 400 pounds of ethylene oxide in an entire year.

Representatives for Sterilization Services of Virginia did not respond to calls seeking comment.

The new rules required not only sterilizers but also chemical plants and steel facilities to monitor for emissions of cancer-causing gases along their property lines by 2027. If certain amounts of the gases got out, the operators had to fix the leaks. Some facilities also had to build special containment systems — akin to giant breadboxes — to reduce gas releases.

Though the facilities would still have to follow pollution limits already in place, the industries fought the E.P.A.’s new mandates, calling them expensive, unnecessary and unworkable. They also challenged the Biden administration’s scientific findings.

“It is critical that regulation of our industry is based on sound science and that those regulations reflect a reasonable assessment of the risks and benefits involved,” Brendan Bradley, a spokesman for the American Chemistry Council, an industry trade group, said in a statement.

The Trump administration did not ask companies to present an exhaustive case for why they deserved a waiver from these new requirements. It was as easy as sending an email to the E.P.A. and invoking the obscure exemption language in the act, a provision that no president had ever used.

Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement the waivers were necessary to protect American manufacturing.

“Exemptions were issued due to crushing Biden-era regulations that required large swaths of our industrial base to adopt technologies that don’t exist outside the imagination of Biden’s E.P.A. bureaucrats,” she said.

Mr. Trump’s decisions rewarded industries that backed his re-election campaign and continued to donate to his pet causes once he won.

AdvaMed boasted earlier this year in a letter to members that its lobbying efforts, which included political contributions to Mr. Trump’s causes, had paid off, saving the industry millions of dollars in upgrades.

“Membership has its privileges,” the group wrote.

The chemical plant in Port Neches, Texas, just south of the meandering Neches River, is a vital cog in American manufacturing. It is among the country’s biggest producers of ethylene oxide.

The plant’s owner, Indorama Ventures, is a major employer in the region and supports local schools, including Groves Middle School. It provides a football training complex through which its chemical pipelines run. It also sponsors the annual Fish-O-Rama Fishing Tournament to raise money for local science and math programs.

The plant also has a long history of releasing toxic pollutants into the community, state records show.

On more than 500 occasions since 2003, it has experienced malfunctions or other failures that resulted in releases of air pollution or toxic chemicals, frequently in violation of its permit, Texas records show.

From his front yard, dotted with baseballs and children's bikes, Cody Coburn can see the flares that burn off excess toxic gases from the plant across the street. Some nights they rattle his windows, suggesting a possible malfunction at the plant.

The incidents leave Mr. Coburn and his wife wondering if they are taking a risk living there with their young sons. “We’ve talked about moving away,” he said.

The violations continued after Indorama, based in Bangkok, purchased the facility from the Texas-based Huntsman Corporation in 2020.

A particularly alarming incident occurred in early 2022. A control valve failed, sending 57,000 pounds of pollutants into the air, including ethylene oxide, records show. The discharges continued for nearly a week.

That 2022 incident, and others like it, put Indorama on the radar of E.P.A. officials who were rewriting the rules for chemical plants.

These kinds of facilities had long used models to estimate their emissions. The problem was, no one could say if the estimates were accurate.

The E.P.A. decided to find out. The agency emailed the managers of the Indorama plant and 10 other facilities, ordering them to install temporary devices at the edges of their properties to measure toxins in the air.

Career E.P.A. employees were stunned by the results, said Brenda Shine, then the agency engineer who supervised the data collection.

Based on data provided by the plant, agency staff had estimated the tests for benzene, a gas linked to cancer, would find about 0.02 micrograms per cubic meter of air — a relatively small amount. But the actual air sampling revealed benzene levels nearly 50 times as high. It also found three times as much ethylene oxide in the air as estimated.

Similar conditions were found at other plants, but Indorama’s tests showed the worst results.

The public health implications were enormous.

An additional one in every 500 people who lived near the plant for most of their lives was likely to develop cancer from exposure to ethylene oxide, a March 2024 EPA report concluded. That risk is 20 times the 1-in-10,000 level that the E.P.A. typically considers to be the highest acceptable cancer risk when it evaluates carcinogens.

That cancer threat from the Indorama plant could be cut by 95 percent, the E.P.A. found, if better pollution controls were installed.

“There was a sense of urgency,” said Joseph Goffman, who supervised Ms. Shine’s work as the head of the agency’s air office during the Biden administration. “It really alarmed local communities.”

Indorama executives argued that the E.P.A. had gathered samples while the plant was undergoing maintenance, so the results did not reflect normal operations, records show. But when agency inspectors returned in 2024, they still found ethylene oxide leaking in multiple locations and drifting across the facility’s fence line.

A spokeswoman for Indorama declined to address detailed questions from The Times about the plant and cancer risks because they involve continuing regulatory discussions.

“Indorama Ventures recognizes the importance of protecting the health and well-being of our employees, neighbors and surrounding communities,” Patricia Sakamiti, a company spokeswoman, said in a statement.

The test results were a critical factor in the E.P.A.’s approving the new air toxics rules.

Those rules required Indorama and other facilities to limit leaks from valves and upgrade flares so that they could burn off more toxic gases before they were released. The companies also had to install monitors around a plant’s fence line. The results would be publicly posted, letting neighbors see what they were breathing.

The E.P.A. estimated that similar improvements would cost about $440 million to install and $163 million a year to maintain for all affected facilities. That would constitute less than 1 percent of the industry’s national sales.

For that price, millions of people who live near these plants would be at a lower cancer risk, the agency concluded.

Indorama said the E.P.A. had acted “beyond its statutory authority” when it required the fence line tests and that the demands were based on a “flawed risk assessment.” Executives from plants that use ethylene oxide to sterilize medical devices, including the one outside Richmond, joined the protests.

So did companies like U.S. Steel, which operates a facility in Clairton, Pa., near Pittsburgh. The plant bakes coal at up to 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit, turning it into coke, an ingredient in steel making.

U.S. Steel, in a statement at the time, said it was committed to working with the E.P.A. in supporting regulations that were “well grounded in law” and science. “Unfortunately, the 2024 coke rules do not meet these criteria,” it said.

Eleven days into the second Trump administration, Lee Zeldin, the newly sworn-in E.P.A. administrator, received a request from the American Chemistry Council and American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, the two biggest trade groups for the chemical industry.

They wanted Mr. Zeldin, a former Republican lawmaker, to push the president to give them relief from the Biden-era rules.

The trade associations, in their petition, laid the groundwork for the Trump administration to intervene for national security reasons, arguing that the new requirements could cause them to curb or cease production. “National security includes economic security and protection of domestic production of chemicals vital to public health,” the petition said.

The chemical and medical device industries were also busy writing a flurry of checks to Mr. Trump’s causes.

AdvaMed sent $125,000 to his inauguration fund and $1 million to MAGA Inc., one of Mr. Trump’s campaign affiliates. The latter donation was made on the same day in April 2025 that AdvaMed’s chief executive, Scott Whitaker, attended a candlelight dinner with Mr. Trump at his Mar-a-Lago resort.

“Yes, I met with President Trump and was grateful for the opportunity to introduce our lifesaving industry to him,” Mr. Whitaker said in a statement, adding that ethylene oxide did not come up.

One of the E.P.A. officials who was copied on the request for regulatory relief was Mr. Szabo, a senior adviser who was awaiting confirmation to lead the agency’s powerful Office of Air and Radiation, which oversees regulations intended to curb toxic pollution.

In Mr. Trump’s first administration, Mr. Szabo had served as a White House lawyer, helping review new regulations. But before that term ended, he moved to the lobbying world, representing oil and gas companies, chemical manufacturers and coal-burning electric utilities.

His clients included AdvaMed, and Mr. Szabo secured private meetings with the E.P.A. and the White House through 2024 to help the medical device industry fight the Biden-era changes, records show. Before Mr. Trump’s re-election, Mr. Szabo also helped draft the E.P.A. chapter in Project 2025, the conservative blueprint for a second Trump term.

From his new perch within the E.P.A., Mr. Szabo began participating in gatherings at the agency’s headquarters with former clients and working on the industry’s wish list, according to emails reviewed by The Times.

Brigit Hirsch, an E.P.A. spokeswoman, said in a statement that an ethics agreement Mr. Szabo signed last year permitted him to work on “general” matters that affected various industry players but not “particular” matters that narrowly affected his former clients until one year passed.

E.P.A. officials held at least 40 meetings with chemical industry executives in 2025, agency entrance logs show.

Mr. Szabo coordinated these efforts with two deputies who had joined the E.P.A. after stints in industry: Abigale Tardif, a former lobbyist for the oil refiner Marathon Petroleum and American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, and Alexander Dominguez, a former American Petroleum Institute lobbyist.

Mr. Szabo also reached out to Emily Underwood, a senior White House lawyer, suggesting that the president could invoke the Clean Air Act exemptions, documents show.

“Thanks Aaron! Can we just see the copy for POTUS’ proposed mention of/remarks on this?” Ms. Underwood responded.

Ms. Underwood, when reached by phone, told The Times that the agency took the lead on these efforts: “The best person to talk to on that would be Aaron Szabo at the E.P.A.”

Mr. Szabo declined to comment. Ms. Tardif did not respond to requests for comment.

The same day that he corresponded with Ms. Underwood, Mr. Szabo appeared before the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee for his confirmation hearing. It was Ash Wednesday, and Mr. Szabo, a Catholic, bore a cross of ashes on his forehead.

Mr. Szabo told senators that he had a personal stake in clean-air rules because he had cystic fibrosis, a lung disease exacerbated by air pollution.

“Growing up, I could feel the impact of poor air quality in my lungs,” he said.

A week later, the E.P.A. created a special inbox to receive requests for waivers from the rules. Companies soon flooded the agency with submissions.

To understand the newfound power of the chemical industry inside the E.P.A., consider a meeting in May 2025 at the agency’s satellite offices in North Carolina.

Nearly a dozen senior chemical industry executives flew in and gathered in a large conference room. Another 30 industry members joined on a video call. The participants represented some of the industry’s biggest players, including Dow, BASF and Huntsman.

The agenda was set by the chemical industry rather than its regulators.

“To provide some structure to our discussions, we prepared the attached agenda,” Leslie Bellas, a vice president for regulatory affairs at American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, wrote to the E.P.A. team.

The de facto moderator was Brendan Mascarenhas, a lobbyist for the American Chemistry Council, according to meeting minutes and participants.

Industry officials were not shy about their demands then and at follow-up gatherings with E.P.A. officials, the minutes show.

First, they wanted the E.P.A. to rescind its scientific finding that ethylene oxide was much more likely to cause cancer than previously thought. The determination had formed a legal basis for many regulations, and with it gone, the rules would fall like dominoes.

Companies also wanted to roll back requirements for fence line monitors. And in the event of a leak, they wanted to keep plants running longer before shutting down for repairs.

That same month, the chief executives of Dow, Chemours, OxyChem and the American Chemistry Council gathered with Mr. Zeldin at his office in Washington.

Chris Jahn, the head of the chemistry council, wrote on social media afterward that they discussed transforming the E.P.A. so that it focused on “pro-growth policies,” while also “protecting human health and the environment.”

By July 2025, when Mr. Trump had still not granted the waivers, executives grew anxious.

The deadline for the first of the new pollution controls was only a year away, and it would take nearly that long to install the necessary equipment. So the chief executives of Dow, BASF, Eastman Chemical and Huntsman wrote a letter directly to Mr. Trump and shared it with the E.P.A.

“We write to bring to your attention the urgent need for action on requests submitted earlier this year for Presidential Exemptions under the Clean Air Act to provide relief from unnecessary and ineffective obligations imposed by E.P.A.,” they wrote.

Three days later, on July 17, Mr. Trump began answering their pleas.

A series on the Trump administration’s historic weakening of environmental protections, and the resulting increase in air and water pollution.

He issued his first exemptions for 50 chemical plants and 40 sterilizers. His order said that “the current compliance timeline would undermine our national security,” and that the sterilizer rule relied on “technologies that do not exist in a commercially viable form,” even though the breadbox-like enclosures were already in use in some states.

The E.P.A. pointed to Mr. Trump when asked about the exemptions. “This decision was made by the White House, as it is a presidential authority,” Mr. Szabo wrote to one Texas Republican lawmaker.

Then, two of the former lobbyists within the E.P.A. turned to weakening the underlying rules.

One was Ms. Tardif, who had represented the oil refiner Marathon Petroleum in meetings at the E.P.A. as recently as December 2024. In a June 2025 email, an official at American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers thanked her for “productive discussions” about “reconsideration” of the chemical plant rules and copied an official at Marathon.

The other was Mr. Szabo, who asked his staff this spring to strike the same provisions from the sterilizer rule that he had once represented AdvaMed in opposing, including the requirement to install the enclosures.

He delivered an even bigger victory to his former clients by summer.

In a memo dated Aug. 13, E.P.A. staff members warned Mr. Szabo that removing the fence line monitoring requirement for all affected chemical plants would be “difficult to justify” in court. They also noted that the Clean Air Act required the E.P.A. to address “air toxics that pose the greatest potential health threat,” including those tied to cancer.

Despite those warnings, Mr. Szabo issued the order to kill the mandate that same day.

It would be one of Mr. Szabo’s final acts at the agency. This month he resigned and took another job at a law firm that has represented industry groups in their challenges to some of the same Clean Air Act rules.

In Clairton, smokestacks at U.S. Steel’s facility release clouds of steam and chemicals. Thanks to the Trump administration, the plant no longer has to curb some of its toxic emissions, at least for now.

Melanie Meade’s house, in her family for generations, sits on a ridge overlooking the plant. In her backyard, it often smells like rotten eggs or burning rubber, and time outdoors makes her feel lightheaded.

Ms. Meade said she knew she faced an elevated risk of cancer, which killed her older sister and several of her neighbors. But she cannot afford to buy a comparable house elsewhere. So she stays.

A spokesman for U.S. Steel, Andrew Fulton, said in an email that Clairton Coke Works had never been fined for exceeding benzene emissions standards. The company plans to invest up to $2.5 billion in its plants in southwestern Pennsylvania, but none of it will be spent on new pollution controls in Clairton, Mr. Fulton said.

“It would be premature for U.S. Steel or any other regulated company to invest in controls while the rule is under reconsideration,” he said.

In Groves, Texas, which sits adjacent to the Indorama plant, some residents were surprised to learn that Mr. Trump had waived requirements designed to protect their health. Their reactions were mixed.

Chris Borne, the mayor of Groves, appreciates Indorama.

“I have full faith in our facilities where I live,” said Mr. Borne, an electrician who has handled jobs in many of the area’s chemical plants. “Sometimes the rule makers, they go too far.”

Others were angry about the administration’s moves.

“Making things great again — I thought that meant making all things great, including our health,” said Lance Bridges, who voted for Mr. Trump in 2016.

As Mr. Bridges spoke, his 22-year-old daughter pushed a toy scooter carrying his granddaughter in front of their house.

A few weeks later, the Indorama plant had another accidental discharge. Gases started seeping into the community at 6 a.m. on Sept. 11, shortly before students began streaming into school.

State records show that the leak continued for eight hours.

Andrew Chavez and Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: 5 Takeaways From Our Investigation of Trump’s Waivers for Polluters
item.description:
They are among the biggest sources of cancer-causing pollution in the United States: chemical manufacturers, steel-making plants, facilities that sterilize medical devices.

In 2024, they were required to take steps to reduce their toxic emissions. That all changed when President Trump returned to office and gave them a pass.

It was the biggest presidential intervention in the Clean Air Act since the bedrock environmental law was enacted more than 50 years ago.

Mr. Trump has gone further than any president in dismantling regulations designed to protect the environment, resulting in dirtier air and water. Even so, his aid to specific polluters stands out. To understand these efforts, The New York Times reviewed more than 10,000 pages of government documents and conducted more than 70 interviews.

Here are five takeaways from our investigation.

Mr. Trump exempted 202 facilities in 39 states and Puerto Rico from new regulations that the Environmental Protection Agency had adopted during the Biden administration.

The new rules came about because the Clean Air Act requires the E.P.A. to periodically study the latest pollution controls and impose them if they are affordable and effective.

The rules required medical sterilizers, chemical plants and steel facilities to monitor for emissions of cancer-causing gases along their property lines by 2027. If they detected certain levels of the gases escaping into communities, they had to fix the leaks. And they had to post the findings publicly, so that neighbors could see what was in the air.

When it comes to chemical manufacturers, the government estimated companies would have to spend about $440 million to install equipment to comply with the new rules and about $163 million each year after that.

That would amount to less than 1 percent of the chemical industry’s annual sales.

The chemical industry criticized the rules as expensive, unnecessary and unworkable. Its lawyers filed petitions with Congress, the E.P.A. and federal courts to overturn or at least delay the regulations. It also challenged the scientific findings underpinning the policies.

Yet the industry lost again and again as agency officials and the courts concluded its claims lacked merit.

As soon as Mr. Trump returned to office, though, the industry players saw an opportunity to change their fortunes. Less than two weeks after the inauguration, trade groups asked the E.P.A. administrator, Lee Zeldin, to push Mr. Trump to exempt them from the rules. A trade association for the medical device industry, which uses ethylene oxide, donated to Mr. Trump’s inauguration fund and to his campaign affiliate, MAGA Inc.

They kept their pressure up until they got what they wanted.

On July 14, 2025, the chief executives of Dow, BASF, Eastman Chemical and Huntsman Corporation sent a letter directly to Mr. Trump, and shared it with the E.P.A.

“We write to bring to your attention the urgent need for action on requests submitted earlier this year for presidential exemptions under the Clean Air Act to provide relief from unnecessary and ineffective obligations imposed by E.P.A.,” they wrote.

Three days later, on July 17, Mr. Trump began answering their pleas.

Never before had a president let specific polluters off the hook with the stroke of his pen.

An obscure provision of the Clean Air Act allows the president to issue exemptions from rules if a manufacturing disruption would undermine national security and the technology needed to comply is not widely available. President Richard M. Nixon signed the law in 1970, but the provision had never been invoked.

Yet Mr. Trump approved the requests for waivers even though the technology was readily accessible and the industry’s national security arguments had little detail to substantiate them, according to documents reviewed by The Times.

The E.P.A. set up a special email inbox for requests for exemptions. Companies flooded the agency with submissions.

The waivers were good for two years, with the possibility of an extension. The reprieve for the companies gave Mr. Trump time to stock the E.P.A. with former industry insiders who worked from within to gut the rules altogether.

For example, Mr. Trump nominated a former top lobbyist for the Advanced Medical Technology Association, or AdvaMed, a powerful trade association, to lead the agency’s air regulation office. The former lobbyist, Aaron Szabo, had been helping the industry fight the regulations under the Biden administration. Now he oversaw the effort to rewrite them. Documents reviewed by The Times indicate that Mr. Szabo helped handle the waiver requests and then pushed employees to pull back on enforcement.

The president’s decisions were a huge victory for an industry that backed his re-election campaign and continued to donate to his pet causes once he took office again.

AdvaMed boasted earlier this year in a letter to members that its lobbying efforts, which included political contributions to Mr. Trump’s causes, had paid off in the form of curbs on air toxics rules that saved companies millions of dollars in upgrades per plant.

“Membership has its privileges,” the group wrote.

That is how many Americans live within three miles of at least one facility that received a permission slip to pollute from Mr. Trump.

Before the E.P.A. finalized the new rules in 2024, it held meetings to warn people who lived near facilities that sterilize medical devices about the elevated cancer risks.

These facilities use ethylene oxide, a colorless, sweet-smelling, toxic gas. The agency’s research had found that long-term exposure to ethylene oxide increased the risk of leukemia, multiple myeloma and other types of cancer, particularly for people living close to where the gas is produced or used.

“You see these pretty buildings and you think they’re OK,” said Wayne Powell, who lives a five-minute drive from a sterilizer outside of Richmond, Va., that resembles an ordinary warehouse. “But you don’t know that they’re harboring things that are hazardous to our health.”

item.title: Attention, Passengers: High Airfares May Be Here to Stay
item.description:
Airfares soared because of the war with Iran. It’s looking increasingly likely that prices won’t come down anytime soon.

Tensions in the Middle East have risen in recent days, pushing up oil prices. But even if the war ended and fuel costs fell, ticket prices could remain stubbornly high.

Travelers, particularly affluent ones who buy high-end seats, have been undeterred so far by the higher prices. Other costs for the airlines are up. And they are facing less competition. Spirit Airlines, which once offered tickets for less than $100, shut down this spring, and other low-cost carriers are struggling.

“It’s expensive to fly airplanes,” Scott Kirby, the chief executive of United Airlines, told Wall Street analysts in a conference call on Wednesday. Most companies in his industry will lose money this year, so fares will have to remain high, he said. “I think the tide has to rise for everyone or those airlines simply won’t exist.”

In September, airfares were 22 percent more expensive than a year earlier, according to federal data. The average cost of a round-trip Thanksgiving flight within the United States is currently about $389, about 39 percent more than it was at this time last year, according to Hopper, a booking app known for its price-tracking features. Similar flights for Christmas are averaging $452, up 22 percent from a year ago.

Fuel typically accounts for about 25 to 30 percent of an airline’s operating costs, behind only wages and employee benefits. So when jet fuel prices nearly doubled in March, airlines raised fares. Jet fuel prices fell in the spring, but have steadily climbed since July. Today, they are about as high as they have been since the United States and Israel began attacking Iran on Feb. 28.

American Airlines and United each said this past week that their fuel costs in the quarter that ended in September were nearly $1.9 billion higher than the same period last year. United said it had recaptured 72 percent of that cost, though it expected to recover the rest eventually.

Other expenses have increased, too. Landing fees and airport rents were up 9 to 14 percent in the third quarter from a year earlier for several airlines.

Airlines are also paying employees more after negotiating new labor contracts with pilots, flight attendants and other workers in recent years. American, Delta Air Lines and United each spent 7 to 10 percent more on salaries, wages and benefits during the first nine months of this year than they did in the same period in 2025.

Airline executives say ticket price increases are long overdue to cover such costs. Adjusted for inflation, the average fare for a flight within the United States last year was 25 percent cheaper than a decade ago, according to federal data, which does not include fees.

In the past, travelers could expect fares to come down once fuel prices fell. As costs dipped, airlines would have cut prices to win over as many customers as possible.

But the industry is changing. Carriers are less concerned with filling planes and more so with attracting customers who will pay for more comfortable seats and better service.

That is, in part, because budget carriers are no longer the powerhouses they once were. A little over a decade ago, Spirit had some of the industry’s highest profit margins. But Spirit shut down in May, after struggling with high costs and competition, notably from larger airlines that offered no-frills “basic economy” tickets to lure customers from Spirit and other low-cost carriers. The airline’s demise already appears to have contributed to higher fares in some places.

Southwest Airlines, which also had a reputation for bringing down prices, is remaking itself in the mold of American, Delta and United by charging bag fees and removing seats from its Boeing 737 planes to make space for more expensive ones with extra legroom.

Delta and United are by far the most profitable airlines today because they have focused on selling premium seats and keeping customers loyal by offering big spenders generous perks. The sale of economy cabin seats — once the bread-and-butter of airlines — now accounts for less than half of Delta’s revenue. American has said leisure travelers are buying nearly two-thirds of the airline’s premium and business-class seats.

John Dalton is one of the customers airlines covet. Mr. Dalton, an actor who teaches theater appreciation to older people in Miami, has always loved to travel. He first bought a business-class ticket a decade ago for a trip to Europe to celebrate overcoming cancer. Today, he tries to fly business on most long trips, even if it means reducing other spending.

“I was like, ‘OK, I’ll splurge on getting a business class seat,’ and then I liked it, which was the curse,” he said. “All of a sudden, you’re like, ‘Oh, this is the way it could be,’ to the point that I dread having to fly coach.”

Generally, customers have accepted double-digit fare increases with a “limited amount of resistance,” Delta’s chief executive, Ed Bastian, said on an earnings call this month.

And while budget travelers have pulled back a bit, some airline executives said they were not too anxious about losing a few customers. American, Alaska Airlines and United recently said they were flying slightly emptier planes while collecting much more revenue. That is “a trade we would make every day,” United’s chief commercial officer, Andrew Nocella, said on the earnings call.

The question now is whether airlines will be able to resist the urge to lower prices to fill those seats.

Some industry experts said airline executives were using their public statements, especially their conference calls with analysts, to signal to investors and one another that they did not plan to lower fares.

“They will willingly discount-shame anybody who has the temerity to try to break price,” said Robert Mann, an industry consultant and former airline executive.

Mr. Mann said there are fewer airlines in the United States than in the past, which means the remaining companies may feel less pressure to lower fares.

Airlines cycle between flooding the market with seats and retrenching. In 2024, carriers were optimistic about demand and significantly increased the number of flights they offered during the summer. The resulting glut of seats forced companies like Spirit to cut prices. That contributed to Spirit’s downfall, which has reduced the number of seats for sale, thus easing the pressure on airlines to lower fares.

Over a longer stretch of time, the balance could again swing back in the favor of travelers.

This month, Boeing received long-delayed federal approval to start delivering the largest version of its 737 Max plane. United and Alaska are expected to receive 19 and 22 of those planes next year. Southwest also expects to start receiving the smallest Max variant, which was certified in August.

And if the economy weakens and stocks fall sharply, many affluent travelers may rethink their spending on travel, opting for fewer trips, downgrading to economy seats or shopping around for lower fares.

Even travelers like Mr. Dalton have their limits. As major airlines start offering “basic business” fares that strip away perks like lounge access or extra checked bags, he is becoming more willing to shop around.

“It makes me feel less loyal to an airline,” he said, “if they’re nickel-and-diming everything.”

item.title: C.E.O.s Say the A.I. Rollout Is Going Well. Employees Feel Differently.
item.description:
By Jordyn Holman

When it comes to artificial intelligence, chief executives and their work forces aren’t seeing eye to eye.

Corporate leaders, increasingly in earnings calls and interviews, tout productivity gains and say they are doing right by their workers as they roll out the technology.

But workers are much more concerned about being supplanted, and they don’t trust their company’s executives.

A survey from the Milken Institute-Harris Poll Listening Project recently found that more than two-thirds of business leaders expect they will be better off financially in five years because of A.I., while just 27 percent of the U.S. work force felt the same way — a whopping 41 point gap.

Workers also see less A.I. transformation than leadership does. Nearly three-fourths of leaders say A.I. has significantly changed the way work is done, compared with 58 percent of entry and midlevel employees, according to a report released this month from the Wharton School.

“We have corner offices and cubicles, driving the same economy, but living in completely different realities,” John Gerzema, C.E.O. of the Harris Poll, said in an email. “There is a gulf in hope between what leaders think A.I. could bring to companies and what employees feel it is taking away from them.”

What might be worse is that C.E.O.s don’t seem to recognize the disconnect, or that they’re losing the trust of their workers.

For example: Just 15 percent of C.E.O.s said they were concerned about how their approach to A.I. could erode their employees’ trust, according to a survey released this month by consultancy BCG. But 40 percent of workers said their C.E.O. has not been transparent enough about the impact of A.I. on their role and career trajectory.

The distrust doesn’t make for a successful transformation, said Julia Dhar, the leader of the North American people and organization practice at BCG and an author of the study.

“You will not get the people you need to start using it more intensively to do so,” Dhar said. “And there is a very good chance you will get backsliding or regression from other people.”

Hemant Taneja, who leads the venture capital firm General Catalyst, said the findings of the BCG report were not surprising, but relatable.

“When there’s more ambiguity, you need to over-communicate,” Taneja said in an interview. “I’m feeling the pain of that in my own business as well.”

He said he has been working to build trust by explaining his decisions around A.I. to employees and founders, especially when they change.

“You have to be vulnerable about the fact that we don’t have all the answers,” Taneja said. “We directionally know where to go, but we don’t know all the answers, and so it’s OK to change assumptions and change your mind.” Dhar said one C.E.O. she knows starts frank discussions around A.I. by asking his frontline employees, “What is the silliest thing we do at this company?” This approach works, she said, because it’s not judgmental, and the C.E.O. doesn’t have to agree on it or make a promise to look into it further.

“But you’ve given people a really easy way to make their voice heard,” she said.

Tim Walsh, chief executive of consultancy KPMG, says when he travels to offices in different cities he makes a point to sit down with both the partners in the business as well as employees.

“I need to understand how they’re feeling, I need to understand how the technology is being received and I need to understand their concerns,” Walsh said in an interview. “I will tell you it’s hard to get it at my level.”

Walsh said he hasn’t mastered the art of getting rank-and-file employees to open up completely in front of him. KPMG relies on anonymous employee surveys as a platform where more junior employees can feel freer to complain.

Despite a struggle to build trust with workers around A.I., there is a bright spot for chief executives. The distrust Americans have toward C.E.O.s and more specifically their own C.E.O. is less than it is for other institutions in American life like media outlets, NGOs and government, according to the Edelman Trust Barometer, which has been measuring trust levels in for the past 26 years.

The research also found that U.S. employees appreciated hearing from their leaders about A.I. even in instances when they didn’t have all the answers.

“People are often very realistic about a business reality and their requests are often quite humble,” Dhar said. “They say, I would just hope the leaders are able to be honest and specific about the changes that we are making and the reason behind them.”

Tesla and SpaceX are considering a merger. Elon Musk confirmed on Tuesday that the boards of each company have formed a special committee to explore a tie-up. Musk cautioned that any such proposal would require approval from at least 50 percent of all outstanding shares in Tesla.

Researchers discovered a widespread security vulnerability. Companies and government agencies scrambled to patch the major bug in PHP, an open-source programming language that is critical to internet architecture. The vulnerability was detected with the help of A.I., but bad actors could also use A.I. to exploit it.

Mark Zuckerberg struck a deal to pay California’s potential billionaire tax. Zuckerberg negotiated with the company’s board over how he would pay the one-time 5 percent tax on all holdings. Meta responded by creating a new class of shares that allows him to raise billions without compromising his voting power in the company. In return, he agreed to stay in the state for eight more years, except for under some conditions. The new share class will also let Meta raise more money for its A.I. ambitions.

More big deals: Saudi Arabia postponed its big investment conference amid concerns about security. Trump asked Elon Musk to restore Ukraine’s access to the Starshield satellite communications network. And next week will be a big test for the strength of A.I. financing: Anthropic is expected to file its public I.P.O. prospectus within the next few days, and Google, Microsoft and Amazon report earnings.

Meta’s new A.I. team has 50 engineers for every manager. Airbnb’s C.E.O., Brian Chesky, has popularized the delegation-shunning strategy of staying in “founders mode.” While Uber, Meta, Amazon and more have been aggressively laying off middle managers.

In the midst of what has been termed “the Great Flattening,” hierarchy seems to have few defenders. But Nir Halevy, a professor of organizational behavior at Stanford University, argues that levels of management are actually quite useful — when done right. He talked with Sarah Kessler about his new book, “Level Up.” The interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Why don’t flat organizations work?

It’s difficult to scale. And we all engage in social comparisons. Those tendencies don’t disappear just because we decided to create a flat structure.

There’s a lot of evidence showing that informal hierarchies are very swift and powerful in the tendency to emerge.

What do you want instead of an informal hierarchy?

You want it to be based on common values. We want to create a hierarchy that provides people with multiple pathways to contribute and thrive and ascend and lead.

What usually makes the hierarchy dysfunctional?

One, if they’re ultracompetitive. And that competition might manifest in withholding help or may actually lead to sabotage.

Broken hierarchies are unjust. You really deserve a promotion, but you’re not going to get the promotion because the boss’s nephew got it. You get arbitrary decisions that are not justified and not explained.

And instability. You will experience a lot of unpredictable, swift changes. People leave, there is a lot of turnover, retention becomes a struggle and people feel a sense of threat and stress and paranoia.

Is there a size at which you don’t need hierarchy?

One of the examples I discuss in the book is Valve, which makes video games and has a few hundred employees. It presents itself to the world as a flat organization. If you go to their landing page, they say, We’ve been boss free since 1996. But they do distinguish based on salaries. They are not all receiving the same information. They have informal hierarchies.

But if I have just like 10 people, is it reasonable to say I’m the boss, but everybody else is on the same level?

You can say that. The question is the extent to which the people actually think that it’s true or fair.

Does A.I. change hierarchy? Do we still need middle management?

Initiatives to use technology to flatten organizations are definitely on the rise. But there is a neglect of the multiple functions that people, let’s say middle management, are doing.

If people erroneously believe their managers are only aggregating information from the bottom, transferring it upward, or taking kind of directions from the top and transferring it downward, then they might mistakenly believe that A.I. can replace employees.

This question comes from a recent edition of the newsletter. Click an answer to see if you’re right. (The link is free.)

Bandcamp

Apple Music

Spotify

All of the above

Thanks for reading! We’ll see you Monday.

We’d like your feedback. Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.

item.title: Noah Adams, Longtime Host of ‘All Things Considered,’ Has Died at 84
item.description:
Noah Adams, a longtime host of NPR’s “All Things Considered” whose quiet baritone and empathetic ear brought listeners stories of back-roads America not often heard on the national airwaves, died on Oct. 16 at his home in Yellow Springs, Ohio. He was 84.

The cause was complications of a benign brain tumor removed eight years ago, his wife, Neenah Ellis, said.

Mr. Adams was a postman’s son from Kentucky who never finished college, and he worked hard to lose the Appalachian accent that he knew conjured up negative stereotypes about his native region.

But he never lost his respect for rural and working-class Americans, and he delighted in leaving Washington, where NPR is based, to travel around the country interviewing miners, farmers, single mothers and factory workers.

In the morning meetings, where the day’s events and newsmakers were discussed, Ms. Ellis, who worked in production at NPR, recalled, “He was looking for who was yearning, who was in pain, who needed help out in the country.”

Mr. Adams abhorred interviewing officials with pat talking points, though that was often part of his job as host of the weeknight edition of “All Things Considered,” NPR’s flagship news and interview show, a position he held for 18 years. He preferred to seek out regular people whose lives were affected by national events.

“The best stories come from west of the Potomac,” he once said.

His respect for his sources came through in interviews of those unaccustomed to a microphone.

“He was wonderfully warm and conversational with people,” said Melissa Block, another host of “All Things Considered,” who worked as a producer for Mr. Adams early in her career. “I don’t know that anyone talking with him would think, ‘Oh, the interview is about to start.’ It would just be a conversation.”

From 1982 to 1987, Mr. Adams’s co-host on “All Things Considered” was Susan Stamberg, an emotive, brainy New Yorker. It was a matchup that showed how opposites attract.

“He is the most genuine, uncontrived voice in broadcasting,” Ms. Stamberg wrote in the introduction to a 1992 book that Mr. Adams wrote about a year of his work for NPR.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

After a short hiatus, he returned to host “All Things Considered” with Robert Siegel and Linda Wertheimer from 1989 until 2002.

“He was a very private and shy person,” Mr. Siegel said in an interview.

After Mr. Adams wrote a book about learning to play the piano at 51, “Piano Lessons” (1997), Mr. Siegel recalled Mr. Adams’s distress at realizing that he would have to perform on his book tour: “I watched him at a Borders, and he was terrified. But he loved what he did. He pulled it off very beautifully.”

During his time away from NPR, from 1987 to 1989, Mr. Adams was recruited to host a replacement show for the much-loved “A Prairie Home Companion,” whose creator, Garrison Keillor, had left. The replacement, “Good Evening,” was another folksy variety show broadcast live from a theater in St. Paul, Minn. It was enlivened by Mr. Adams’s essays about the community on the St. Croix River where he had settled, but it struggled to replicate Mr. Keillor’s audience.

The show lasted less than a year, and Mr. Adams announced his departure shortly before it ended. “I never felt people were saying, ‘Gee, that’s not Garrison Keillor,’” he later said somewhat defensively.

Noah Donald Adams was born on Sept. 15, 1942, in Ashland, Ky., the elder of fraternal twin boys. His father, Roy Adams, and his mother, Edith (Wellman) Adams, a secretary, divorced soon after, and Noah and his brother, James, were raised by their mother and maternal grandparents.

Noah graduated from Ashland High School (now Paul G. Blazer High School) and attended Eastern Kentucky State College (now Eastern Kentucky University) for 18 months before being asked to leave because he was living in unauthorized off-campus housing and writing term papers for football players.

He knocked around doing various jobs, — including construction and car sales, before joining the University of Kentucky’s public radio station, WBKY (now WUKY), in Lexington. There, he hosted a progressive rock show and worked the control board for other shows.

After writing a letter to NPR, he was hired in 1975 as a production assistant on “All Things Considered,” which had been introduced four years earlier. In 1978, he became a weekend co-host for the show.

A 90-minute documentary that he co-wrote about the mass suicide at Jonestown in Guyana in 1978, “Father Cares: The Last of Jonestown” (1981), received wide notice for its innovative format and subject. It was based on 900 hours of recordings that the cult leader Jim Jones and his followers had made before their deaths. Mr. Jones’s voice was so chilling, The Minneapolis Star Tribune noted, that “a listener might cling to the rational tone of narrator Noah Adams as to the hand of a friend.”

Though he preferred feature reporting, Mr. Adams did not shy away from hard news at home or abroad. He won an award from the Overseas Press Club of America in 1994 for work he did in Serbia on the roots of the country’s national extremism.

On Sept. 11, 2001, he was on the air from the morning until after dark, updating millions of listeners about the terrorist attacks. He called it the most important day of his career, when he could “feel the audience” intent on understanding the shocking events, Ms. Ellis said.

The following year, Mr. Adams took a leave of absence to research a book about the Wright brothers, one of five nonfiction books he wrote. When he returned, it was as a contributing correspondent on NPR’s national desk. He roamed widely but regularly returned to stories in Appalachia.

Ms. Ellis, who married Mr. Adams in 1987, recalled visiting Appalachia for the first time with him. They were on assignment — she was his producer — and he instructed her and an engineer on how to approach strangers wary of outsiders. You don’t knock on their doors, he told them: “You drive up, get out of the car and stand there until they come out.”

Mr. Adams’s first two marriages ended in divorce. In addition to Ms. Ellis, he is survived by his brother.

Among the thousands of stories that Mr. Adams reported, the one that got the most enthusiastic response was when he visited a New York recording studio and sang a wobbly version of the Eagles song “Take It to the Limit.”

He played the tape on the air for Ms. Stamberg, who squealed, “It’s adorable!”

One of the hundreds of listeners who wrote in said, “I was getting ready to drop out of law school and we were thinking about getting a divorce, but if you have the courage to stand in that studio and play it for Susan on the radio, then I know we can do anything we really set our minds to.”
